# Components and assemblies

Build like a designer: smallest components first, then assemblies of them.

- `shape.create` with `"definition": true` makes a component that is only placed through instances.
- `assembly.create` makes an assembly definition; `assembly.instance.create { of, parent, name, at:[x,y,z] mm, rotation:[rx,ry,rz] (degrees about X, then Y, then Z, as Solid.rotate), properties }` places a component or assembly inside an assembly (`parent`), or at the top of the project (no parent). A definition shows in the person's view only through instances: finish an assembly by placing it at the top (`./ise look` draws a definition either way; the person's view does not, and `./ise check` warns about assemblies placed nowhere).
- Every instance of a definition shows the same design: edit the definition (`shape.set_params`, `shape.update`) and all of them change. Say so when you do it ("this changes all 12 hotel floors").
- An instance can give its shape values of its own and still share the definition (every edit to the program, the library's updates, one BOM line): `assembly.instance.update { target, params: { output: "=Shoulder.angle", length: 120 } }` (also in `assembly.instance.create`; `null` drops one, so the definition's value shows again). A value is a number or a formula (`"=Shoulder.angle"`, `"=Elbow.angle / 2"`; a bare key is another parameter of the same shape), applied after the instance's configuration. A formula that reads a joint follows it live: scrubbing, sweeps, studies and playback evaluate that instance with each step's value. Use it for what differs per placement — a servo's output spline following its own joint, a door's swing, a cable's length — instead of copies; `./ise get <instance>` shows `params` and the view's instance panel shows them as “This instance”. Exports and drawings of a single instance show the definition's values.
- To customise one instance's design (its program, not just values), `assembly.instance.make_unique` first; it returns the new `definition` to edit. Prefer own values (above) when only values differ: a copy stops following the definition.
- `assembly.instance.update` moves, rotates, swaps `of`, renames, or sets `properties` (a value "" removes one). Properties carry facts like `use`, `status` (Available, Reserved, Sold), `owner`, `unit`.
- `assembly.instance.delete` removes an instance (and the joints that name it; what they held stays where it is).
- Repeated parts are instances of one definition, never copies of a program: a thousand screws of one size are one mesh sent once and one draw call (the view draws instances of a geometry as GPU instances, simplified when small on screen), so projects of 10,000 parts stay smooth. A big array (a rack, a facade) goes in one `core.batch` of `assembly.instance.create` steps, or as an assembly of a module placed many times.

Joining components at their connectors (programs declare them with `connector(name, { at, axis, x })`: a shaft's end, a hole, a mounting face; axes point outward):

- `assembly.joint.create { assembly?, type: "fixed"|"hinge"|"slider"|"cylinder"|"ball", a, b, name?, value?, values?, limits?: [min, max], ranges?, offset?, aligned?, free? }` joins two instances of the same assembly (no `assembly`: top-level instances). `a` and `b` are `{ instance, connector }`; `a` may be `"ground"` (the assembly's origin, Z up) or a ground frame `{ at, axis?, x? }`. It puts `b`'s connector on `a`'s, axes opposed (faces meeting; `aligned: true` points them the same way), `offset` mm apart along `a`'s axis, then turns or slides `b` by the value: `angle` (°) for a hinge, `distance` (mm) for a slider, both for a cylinder, `rx`/`ry`/`rz` (°, X then Y then Z of `a`'s frame) for a ball; a fixed joint just seats it (a screw's `Head seat` on a hole, a servo's `Bottom` on its bracket). `value` sets the main value, `values` any by key; a value can be a formula string (`"=Shoulder.angle + 90"`). It is refused with the reason if a connector is missing (the refusal lists those there are) or the joints cannot all hold.
- A joint is also a parameter set named for it: scrub with `parameters.set { target: joint, values: { angle } }`, link with `shape.link_param`, and read from other formulas as `Elbow.angle`. Limits are the parameter's min/max (`assembly.joint.update { target, limits: [min, max] | null }`); a formula that drives a value past them fails that joint, says so, and what it holds waits.
- `assembly.joint.update { target, name?, type?, a?, b?, value?, values?, limits?, ranges?, offset?, aligned?, free? }`; `assembly.joint.delete { target }` (use this, not `core.entity.delete`: what the joint held stays where it is, free).
- Joints that touch make a group. A group reaching the ground hangs from it; otherwise from its anchor, the first instance no joint places (move the anchor and the group follows: bolt the servo to the bracket, then move the bracket). Every other instance in it is held: `assembly.instance.update` refuses to move it and says which joint holds it. Its placement now is `assembly.placed` on the instance (`./ise get`: `at`, `rotation`, `by` the joint that places it). A tree of joints is placed joint by joint; a closed loop (a four-bar of separate links, a part held at two places) is solved so every joint holds, its `free: true` joints taking whatever value the others leave (reported per joint in `placed.values`). Checked: a two-link hinge chain lands on the hand-computed tip within 1e-9 mm; a fixed mate seats a servo exactly (to 1e-12) and follows its bracket tipped on its side; a parallelogram four-bar keeps its coupler level within 1e-6.
- `GET /connectors/<instance id>` lists an instance's connectors where it is now (an assembly's are its instances', "Instance › connector").
- `GET /assembly-motion/<joint id or name>?steps=120&key=&from=&to=&set=` sweeps one joint through its limits (or a full turn; give a slider limits or from/to), the others held (or posed by `set={"Elbow": 30}`): every instance's placement at each step, and every pair of instances that move relative to each other with their closest gap, where, and `clashes` with the range they overlap through (`joined` pairs, joined by a joint, may touch: a shaft in its bore). `gaps=off` skips the gap checks. Checked: an arm swinging into a post clashes from 76° to 104° against 75.75° and 104.25° by hand; at 70° it clears by 3.98 mm (hand: 3.98).
- Requirement `{ kind: "no_clashes_in_motion", joint, parts?, steps?, set?, across?, across_steps? }` runs that sweep on every change (default: the joint's whole assembly, 72 steps) and fails on any clash or binding. `set: { "<joint id>": value }` holds other joints there instead of where they are now (the worst pose: the shoulder low while the elbow folds); `across: ["<joint id>"]` repeats the sweep with those joints stepped through their limits (`across_steps` + 1 values each, default 4), covering the joint space as the interlocks allow it. Add one for every mechanism you assemble, run `./ise check`, and say what it found.
- Checks are kept by what they depend on: each pair of parts' measurement through a sweep is keyed by the two parts' geometry and how one moves against the other, so a change re-measures only the pairs it changed (renaming, properties, a part far away: nothing; a joint posed differently: the pairs it moves). A commit that leaves the moving geometry alone returns in well under a second.
- A shape whose parameter is a formula of a joint's value (a spring whose stretched length and angle follow the arm it pulls on, a bellows, a cable loop; an instance's own value that follows its joint) is evaluated again at every step of a sweep and of `no_clashes_in_motion`, so its clashes are found as it changes (the sweep's notes name it); keep such shapes few and light, each step evaluates them again. Sweeps and studies list them in `flex` with their values at each frame, and the person's view plays them changing (the spring stretches while the shoulder turns): a few frames are evaluated once and blended.
- Interlocks (joint-space limits, as an industrial arm's controller keeps it from folding into itself): `assembly.interlock.create { assembly?, name, description?, zones?: [{ when: { "Shoulder": { max: 40 } }, then: { "Elbow": { max: 100 } } }], tables?: [{ by: "Shoulder", joint: "Elbow", rows: [[0, -60, 100], [40, -60, 100], [60, -60, 120]] }] }`. A zone holds the `then` joints within their ranges whenever every `when` joint stands within its own (`{ min?, max? }` or `[min, max]` with nulls; "Name.key" for another value of a joint); a limit table gives one joint's [min, max] for values of another (rows `[by, min, max]`, linear between rows, held past the ends). `assembly.interlock.update { target, name?, zones?, tables? }`, `assembly.interlock.delete { target }`. Everything that moves the joints respects them: a sweep covers only the values they allow with the other joints where they are (its notes and `allowed` say so; the `no_clashes_in_motion` summary says “interlocks hold Elbow to …”), a motion study or robot path stops where it would enter a forbidden region (binds, with the reason), IK and the reach envelope keep out of them, `parameters.set` / `assembly.pose.apply` / `assembly.robot.move_to` into one is refused with the reason, and the view's joint slider stops at the boundary (shown as “interlock …”). An interlock is created only when the arm stands outside what it forbids. Prefer one to a redesign when a clash happens only in a corner of the joint space (an elbow folding while the shoulder is low): keep the reach elsewhere, and prove it with a `no_clashes_in_motion` holding the worst pose (`set`) or stepping the other joint (`across`) — it fails without the interlock and passes with it.
- `./ise robot <tip> controller [json|arduino] [--out arm_limits.h]` (GET `/robot/<tip>?controller=json|arduino`) writes what the arm's controller firmware needs: each joint's channel (base first), limits and home (the pose called Home, else now), and the interlocks by channel; `arduino` is a C header with `ARM_MIN`/`ARM_MAX`/`ARM_HOME`, `arm_allowed(q)` and `arm_clamp(q)` (limits, then each interlock's held joints into what it allows). Regenerate it whenever joints or interlocks change, and say so.
- Requirement `{ kind: "parameter_range", target, key, min?, max? }`: a parameter of a parameter set, shape or sketch (its value or its formula's result) stays at least `min` and/or at most `max`, re-checked whenever it or anything its formula reads changes. Use it for engineering margins worked out by formula: a servo's stall torque over the holding torque at the worst pose, a spring's longest length against its catalogue maximum, a beam's deflection worked out by hand.
- The person does all of this in an instance's properties: Joints lists each with its value (scrub it and the parts move live), limits, how the faces meet, the gap, Check clashes (a timeline with the clash ranges, playable) and Keep as a requirement; Add joint lights every connector in the view as a small triad to pick the part that moves, then where it goes. Free instances turn with the rotation fields or the rings on the move gizmo.

Mates — constraints on picked geometry, not only declared connectors (FreeCAD Assembly / SolidWorks mates):

- An end can be geometry on an instance: `{ instance, geometry }` with `geometry` (instance's own coordinates, mm) one of `{ type: "face", at, normal }` (a point on a face and its outward normal: found on the part's mesh at every solve — flat → its plane, round → a cylinder's axis and radius, negative for a bore, or a sphere's centre — so the mate follows the part when it changes), `{ type: "edge", points }` (straight → its line; round → its circle's axis), `{ type: "point", at }`, `{ type: "line", at, dir }`, `{ type: "plane", at, normal }`, `{ type: "cylinder", at, dir, radius }`, `{ type: "sphere", at, radius }`, `{ type: "origin" }`. Compute these yourself when you know the geometry; use `face`/`edge` for what was picked in the view. Connectors and ground frames work as ends of mates too (as a plane through the connector facing its axis, or its axis line, matching the other end).
- Mate types for `assembly.joint.create`: `coincident` (point/line/plane on point/line/plane; two planes face each other unless `aligned: true`; `offset` mm gap), `concentric` (two axes one, or two centres), `parallel`, `perpendicular`, `angle` (value `angle` °), `distance` (value `distance` mm: point/line/plane pairs; lines and planes are kept parallel), `tangent` (a cylinder or sphere against a plane, or two round faces; a shaft against a bore's inside uses the bore's negative radius), `lock` (holds the second instance exactly where it is against the first now). An angle or distance not given keeps the one it has now; like joint values they are parameters (scrub, limit, link by formula). A mate refuses geometry it cannot join and says what it needs. `hinge`, `slider`, `cylinder`, `ball` and `fixed` also take geometry ends: they turn or slide about the face's normal or the axis.
- A mate takes away only the freedoms it names: a block's bottom face coincident with a base's top still slides and turns on it. The solver moves what mates hold as little as they need from where it is, so an instance held only by mates can be moved by hand (`assembly.instance.update`) along what they leave free; a lock or a joint holds it outright. Checked: a block picked by its bottom face lands flat on the top (every corner at z = 10 within 1e-7), 3 freedoms left (two slides, a turn about Z); a distance of 15 mm from the left side and a front face flush fix it at (15, 0, 10) within 1e-7 with nothing left free; a 6 mm bore found on its 48-sided mesh to 1e-6 mm, a shaft concentric in it then sliding and turning (2 left); a roller tangent to a floor sits its axis exactly its radius above.
- Couplings make one joint's motion drive another's: `assembly.coupling.create { assembly?, type: "gear"|"belt"|"rack_pinion"|"screw"|"cam"|"ratio", driver, follower (joint names or ids), teeth?: [driver, follower] (gear: turns the other way; belt/chain: same way, teeth or diameters), radius? (rack and pinion: pitch radius mm), lead? (screw: mm per turn), ratio? (follower units per driver unit, any type), offset?, profile?: [[angle °, value], …] (cam, over a turn), driver_key?, follower_key?, name? }`; `assembly.coupling.update { target, ratio?, teeth?, radius?, lead?, profile?, offset?, name? }`, `assembly.coupling.delete { target }`. Before solving, the follower's value is worked out from the driver's; sweeping or scrubbing the follower turns the driver back (not a cam); couplings chain (gear trains); a follower driven past its limits fails and says by which coupling. Checked: 20→40 teeth turn the output −45° for 90° in; a 10 mm pinion slides its rack 15.708 mm per quarter turn; sweeping the output to −90° turns the input to 180°.
- `./ise dof <assembly|top>` (GET `/assembly-dof/<id>`): per group of joined instances, `free` (freedoms nothing determines with every joint at its value: 0 is fully defined), `mobility` (freedoms with joint values let go: 6 for a six-axis arm), each instance's freedoms in words ("turns about (0, 0, 1) through (10, 5, 0)", "slides along (1, 0, 0)"), `redundant` conditions with the joints sharing them (bolted twice: 6, both bolts named; a mate counts only when the others imply all of it), and, when the joints cannot all hold, `conflicting`: each joint whose removal lets the rest hold. Run it after mating parts and tell the person what is still free.

Patterns of instances (live arrays):

- `assembly.pattern.create { seed, type: "linear"|"circular"|"path", count, spacing? (mm, or "=formula"), direction? (default X), count2?, spacing2?, direction2? (a grid), angle? (° between copies) | span? (360: evenly all round), axis?, center?, path?: [[x,y,z], …], closed?, align? (copies turn with the path), name? }` makes count − 1 copies of the seed instance (same definition and configuration: one BOM line) in the seed's assembly; returns `members`. The pattern is a parameter set (`spacing`, `spacing2`, `angle`): scrub or link them and the copies follow; move the seed (or let its joints move it) and they follow; swap its definition or configuration and they show it too. `assembly.pattern.update { target, count?, count2?, spacing?, angle?, direction?, axis?, center?, path?, … }` adds or removes copies. Copies cannot be moved, joined or deleted on their own (join the seed); `assembly.pattern.delete { target, keep? }` removes the copies, or with `keep: true` frees them where they are. Deleting the seed deletes its patterns. Checked: 4 bolts 25 mm apart along Y land at 25/50/75; spacing 30 moves them to 90; four round a centre at 90° steps land exactly.

Saved poses, exploded views and motion studies:

- `assembly.pose.create { assembly?, name, values? }` keeps every joint's value now (or the given `{ "Shoulder": 30, "Wrist": [0, 10, 0] }`); `assembly.pose.apply { target }` puts them back in one change (formula-driven values follow); `assembly.pose.update { target, name?, values?, capture? }`, `assembly.pose.delete { target }`. Make home/park/reach poses for every mechanism.
- `assembly.explode.create { assembly?, name, steps?: [{ instances: [ids], move: [x, y, z], turn?: { axis, angle, at? }, name? }], auto?: { spread } }` saves an exploded view: steps play in order, each moving (and turning) its instances from where the steps before left them; `auto` works the steps out (every part pulled out from the middle; last assembled first when instances carry an assembly `step` property). `assembly.explode.update { target, name?, steps? }`, `assembly.explode.delete`. `./ise exploded <view>` (GET `/explode/<id or name>`) gives every instance's placement after each step and each moved part's trail. The person plays it in the assembly's Exploded views (steps one by one, trails drawn).
- `assembly.motion_study.create { assembly?, name, steps?: [{ joint, to, from?, start?, duration, key? }], poses?: [{ pose, at }], tracks?: [{ joint, key?, keys: [[s, value], …] }], duration?, linear? }`: several joints on one timeline (eased between keys unless `linear`). `./ise study <study> [fps] --out frames.json` (GET `/motion-study/<id or name>?fps=24&gaps=off`) plays it: every instance's placement and every joint's value per frame, clashes with the time range they overlap through, where it binds. The person plays it in the Motion studies panel and exports the frames as PNG images (a zip) or a video.

Robots (any serial chain of joints):

- `./ise robot <tip>` (GET `/robot/<tip instance id or name>?tool=`) finds the chain from the ground (or the anchor) out to the tip instance: its moving joints in order with their limits and values, and where the tool is. The tool point is the tip's connector `tool` (or `point=[x,y,z]` in the tip's coordinates), else a connector called TCP/Tool/Tip, else the tip's middle; its z axis is the approach direction. Joints driven by formulas or couplings (a geared gripper finger) follow and are not part of the chain.
- `./ise robot <tip> fk '{"Shoulder":30}'` (GET `/robot/<tip>/fk?values=`): where the tool goes. `./ise robot <tip> ik x,y,z [--axis 0,0,-1]` (GET `/robot/<tip>/ik?to=&axis=`): joint values within limits that put the tool there (damped least squares from where it is and from spread starts; says how far short when out of reach). `assembly.robot.move_to { tip, to, axis?, tool?, point? }` sets them (refused with the closest it gets when out of reach). `./ise robot <tip> reach [samples]` (GET `/robot/<tip>/reach`): the reach envelope sampled within limits: points, box, nearest and farthest reach from the first joint. `./ise robot <tip> path '[{"pose":"home"},{"to":[x,y,z],"axis":[0,0,-1],"linear":true,"duration":2},{"values":{"Grip":30}}]' [--out file]` (GET `/robot/<tip>/trajectory?through=&fps=`): moves through poses, joint values and tool points (joint moves eased; `linear` ones along a straight tool line), played with every instance and its clashes; reports each waypoint reached. Checked: a two-link arm's tool lands on the hand-computed point (1e-9); IK from straight out finds it again within 1e-4 mm; its farthest reach is 181.1 mm, √(180² + 20²) by hand; a linear move keeps the tool on its line within 0.01 mm.

Interference across an assembly:

- `./ise interference <assembly|instance|shape|top> [clearance]` (GET `/interference/<id>?clearance=`): every pair of placed parts at every depth, each part of a many-part shape on its own, that overlap (mm³, and the overlap's box and middle), touch, or come within `clearance` mm; pairs a joint joins directly are marked `joined` (contact meant; overlap rarely is) and pairs where one is a screw, heat-set insert, nut, PEM self-clinching part or studded standoff are marked `fastener` (threads and inserts overlap what they go into by design), and pairs where one is declared embedded in the other are marked `embedded`; only the rest fail. Checked: two 10 mm cubes 5 mm apart overlap by exactly 500 mm³ (5 × 10 × 10); one 0.5 mm above is reported 0.5 mm away. Run it after assembling and before printing.
- Embedded parts (rebar cast in concrete, an insert moulded into a boss, a threaded bush pressed or glued into its hole, an overmould on its core) overlap their host by design: declare it and interference, `no_collisions` and `./ise fit` count that overlap as meant. In a program: `part("Mesh", bars, { embedded: "Slab" })` (or `["Slab", "Beam"]`; hosts are parts of the same program, a misspelt one is an error) — `rebar(…, { embedded })` passes it on. Between instances: the instance property `embedded` = `"Block"` (or `"Slab, Beam"`) names the instance, shape or part it sits in (`assembly.instance.update { target, properties: { embedded: "Block" } }`). The part must stay inside: where it pokes out of its hosts (bars with no cover, an insert standing proud) it is still reported, with how much (`outside` mm³, `outside_at`), the interference note says where, `no_collisions` fails with that region and fit fails its `embedded` item; a declared part not in its host at all fails too. Stock heat-set inserts, PEM parts and studded standoffs need no declaration (they are fasteners, checked by their own fit items).
- `./ise fit <assembly|instance>` measures each fastener against everything in the project around it, not only its own assembly: a board placed on its own (or in another assembly) that the case's screws clamp is found where the project places it (the head seats on it, the shank's clearance hole in it is checked), while the report stays the assembly's (the board gets no item of its own; a note says how many outside parts were measured; an assembly shown several times is measured where it is first shown). A dowel pin or bearing in a slot or groove (two straight walls, open along their length: a caliper's guide pin in its beam) or lying in an open channel is checked as a sliding fit — `Slot`/`Channel` with the width across, the length free — not as a housing: narrower than the pin fails (it jams), off-centre into a wall fails, machined clearance over max(0.1 mm, 2 % of Ø) or printed over the profile's slide + 0.2 a side warns (it rattles); a pin with only a slot round it and no bore holding it warns.

- `assembly.group.create { name, members }` groups two or more items so they are picked and moved together; nothing about the items changes. `assembly.group.update { target, name?, members? }` renames or changes membership; deleting the group (`core.entity.delete`) ungroups. Several changes that belong together go in one `core.batch { steps: [{ operation, parameters }] }` (one undo step, all or nothing).
